value.overview: The Silvery-throated Jay (Cyanolyca argentigula) is a distinctive mountain jay of Costa Rica and western Panama. It belongs to the crow and jay family and is associated mainly with cool, humid highland forests. Its dark blue plumage, contrasting silvery throat and forehead, and active, social behavior make it a notable bird of Central American montane habitats. It often travels in small groups and searches mossy branches, bromeliads, and foliage for food.
value.classification: The Silvery-throated Jay is a passerine in the family Corvidae, which includes crows, ravens, magpies, and jays. It is one of the blue jays in the genus Cyanolyca.
value.identification: This medium-sized jay is chiefly dark blue, with a conspicuous silvery-white throat extending onto the lower face and forehead. The crown and upperparts are darker blue, while the bill, legs, and feet are black. The iris is dark brown to reddish brown. Juveniles are duller and may show a less distinct facial and throat pattern. Its harsh, nasal calls are useful for detection in dense forest. The species can be confused with other highland Cyanolyca jays, but its silver throat is distinctive within its range.
value.rangeHabitat: The Silvery-throated Jay has a restricted range in Costa Rica and western Panama. In Costa Rica, it occurs in highland regions of the Cordillera Central, including areas around the Irazú and Turrialba volcanoes, and in the Cordillera de Talamanca. It inhabits humid montane evergreen forest, high-elevation oak forest, and forest edges, generally at about 2,000–3,200 meters in Costa Rica. It may use both forest interior and adjoining wooded edges, but is usually associated with relatively cool, mature mountain habitats.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident in Costa Rica and does not undertake regular long-distance migration. Local movements may occur within highland forests in response to food availability or social activity.
value.breeding: The breeding biology of the Silvery-throated Jay is incompletely known. In Costa Rica, breeding activity appears to extend from at least March through June. It is thought to nest in montane forest, but detailed information on nest placement, clutch size, incubation, and parental care remains limited. Pairs or small social groups may remain associated during the breeding period, although the species' broader social and nesting system requires further study.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet is not documented in detail, but known foods include arthropods, fruits, and small vertebrates such as lizards and salamanders. It forages mainly in the forest canopy and subcanopy, moving deliberately through foliage and inspecting bromeliads, mossy branches, and other plant surfaces. At forest edges it may descend lower. Outside the breeding season, it can forage in single-species groups that sometimes include numerous individuals.
value.behavior: The Silvery-throated Jay is active, social, and usually encountered in pairs or groups. Birds move through forest vegetation while giving harsh, nasal calls and may become conspicuous when several individuals travel together. Groups can contain up to roughly 30 birds outside the breeding season. The species generally remains within the forest canopy and subcanopy, but may use edges and nearby wooded habitats. Its calls include rough scolding notes and repeated nasal phrases.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is estimated at approximately 20,000–50,000 mature individuals and is considered stable.
